sections.body_md:
Two directions are \(Q\)-conjugate when their product through \(Q\) vanishes. The matrix \(Q\) is symmetric positive definite and is the Hessian of the quadratic under study. Euclidean orthogonality is the special case in which \(Q\) is the identity. A stretch that makes \(Q\) a non-scalar diagonal matrix splits the two conditions: a right angle on the page need not be conjugacy, and a conjugate pair need not meet at a right angle.

The conjugate-direction method is handed such a set and takes an exact line search along each direction in turn. On a quadratic, the restriction to a line is a parabola. The exact step sits at the bottom of that parabola. Because the directions are conjugate, the parabola in one coefficient does not contain the other coefficients. Each search removes one coefficient of the error, and later searches do not restore it.

In dimension \(n\) there are \(n\) coefficients. After at most \(n\) searches every coefficient is zero, so the point is the minimizer. The count does not depend on the condition number. The condition number changes how a method that lacks conjugacy behaves. It does not change this finite count.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Conjugacy and the exact step are
\[
d_i^T Q d_j = 0\ (i\ne j), \qquad t = -\frac{\nabla f(x)^T d}{d^T Q d}.
\]
The gradient of \(\tfrac{1}{2} x^T Q x + b^T x\) is \(Qx + b\). After the step, the new gradient is orthogonal to \(d\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(Q = \mathrm{diag}(1,\ 3)\), let the gradient be \((8,\ 1)\), and let the direction be \((-2,\ 0)\). The directional derivative is \(8\cdot(-2) = -16\). The curvature is \((-2)\cdot 1\cdot(-2) = 4\). The step length is \(16/4\).

The spar step is 4. The direction is a descent direction because the directional derivative is negative, and the positive curvature makes the parabola open upward. A second direction conjugate to this one would need a product of zero against \(Q\). The first standard-basis direction already has that product equal to zero against \((0,\ 1)\), since the off-diagonal entries are zero.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Calling a Euclidean right angle conjugacy omits \(Q\). The product that has to vanish is \(d_i^T Q d_j\). A second slip is to drop the minus sign in the step length. The directional derivative of a descent direction is already negative, and the minus sign turns the length positive. A third is to divide by \(d^T d\) when \(Q\) is not the identity. The curvature is \(d^T Q d\). A fourth is to expect the gradient to vanish after one search in a plane. The new gradient is orthogonal to the direction just used. The other component can still be large. A fifth is to expect the finite count to fail when the condition number is large. The count is the dimension.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Conjugate gradient does not ask for the directions in advance. It builds the next direction from the new gradient and a multiple of the previous direction, and the multiple is the one that restores conjugacy. On a positive definite quadratic the finite termination remains. The multiple is what replaces the list.
